name: Yara Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grill at a steakhouse near the train station, so my day starts at two and finishes around midnight. The first hour is prep: portioning steaks, making the peppercorn sauce, checking the walk-in fridge. Then from six it's tickets, tickets, tickets, maybe 180 covers on a Friday. I like it, mostly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm when the line is working, when Marco, our head chef, calls an order and four of us move without talking. What wears me out is my feet and the late finish. Daniel, my partner, drives the early bus, so some weeks we only really see each other on Sundays. And the rent went up again in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: robots don't flip steaks, so carry on. Maybe the booking system gets a bit smarter and the rota comes out on time for once. People at work would joke about it for a week and then forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. My worries in that world are the same ones I have now, the rent and whether the steakhouse stays busy. Nothing about AI would change my plans, but my plans are already a bit tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep putting about 150 a month into the savings account. I'd push Marco again for the sous chef spot when Lena, our sous chef, leaves in the spring. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled, if I'm honest. A bit bored by the idea, maybe, but bored is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rent. What happens if it goes up again next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd look at moving further out, probably to the estate past the ring road where Daniel's sister lives. It's 40 minutes on the night bus home, which I'd hate after a midnight finish. We've got about three months of bills saved, so it's not a crisis, just a squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the sous chef spot, how likely is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty-fifty. I'm good, but I'm not the best on the line, and there's a younger guy who's quicker than me on the fryer. If I don't get the sous chef job this year, I'll still have a job, just not a better one.

say: I'd tell people **robots don't flip steaks**, so nothing much changes on the grill.
I'd joke that at least the **rota** might finally come out on time.
think: Privately it would be a **relief**, because my worries stay the ones I already carry.
The real pressures are **rent** and whether the steakhouse stays busy, not AI.
do: Keep putting about **150 a month** into the savings account.
Push the head chef for the **sous chef** spot when it opens in spring.
Look at **moving further out** if the rent rises again next year.
feel: Mostly **settled**, a little bored by the picture, and fine with that.
S0.quote: If I don't get the sous chef job this year, I'll still have a job, just not a better one.
fieldNote: Her plateau answer is about **rent and promotion**, not technology at all.
She rates herself honestly as good but **not the best**, which keeps her hopes modest.
Her late shifts against her partner's **early bus** shifts are a quiet strain she keeps returning to.

steps.text: Keep working the grill and go for the sous chef job in spring
Put about 150 a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say kitchens are fine, it's the office people who should worry. That's what everyone on the line would say, anyway. Maybe I'd post something like that and get a few likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd watch the front of house. If bookings, ordering and the stock list go onto software, the steakhouse needs fewer people upstairs, and the owner starts looking hard at every wage. My grill is safe for now, but the place gets leaner around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until I saw what the owner actually bought before I learned anything new. Once the new ordering system was in and the others were using it, I'd learn it properly, because whoever knows the stock app ends up doing the ordering. And I'd keep the savings going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, just watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya on the front desk, definitely. She does the bookings and takes the phone orders, and she's got a little boy at home. If an app starts taking the bookings, our receptionist Priya loses her job long before anyone on the grill does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Daniel's job, does this picture touch it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I don't think, he drives a bus with people on it. Maybe the timetables and the ticket side go to software. He'd laugh if I even asked him.

say: I'd say **kitchens are fine** and it's the office workers who should worry.
I'd post that line online, because it's what **everyone on the line** believes.
think: Privately I'd watch the **front of house**, where bookings and ordering could move to software.
A leaner steakhouse means the owner looks harder at **every wage**, even if my grill stays safe.
do: Wait to see which **ordering system** the owner actually buys before learning anything.
Learn the **stock app** properly once others use it, since that person ends up ordering.
Keep the **monthly savings** going at the same rate.
feel: **Uneasy** and watchful, but not scared for her own station.
S1.quote: If an app starts taking the bookings, our receptionist Priya loses her job long before anyone on the grill does.
fieldNote: She separates her own **hands-on grill** work from the desk tasks around her very clearly.
Her real worry is for a colleague, the **receptionist with a child**, more than for herself.
Her **steady** streak shows: she would learn new software only after colleagues had proved it.

steps.text: Wait to see which ordering system the steakhouse owner buys
Learn the stock and ordering app once the kitchen uses it
Keep putting 150 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it's scary and leave it there, because I don't like arguing online. At work we'd all say the same thing, that someone still has to cook. I'm not sure anyone would believe it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be counting. AGI in 2028 and robots in 2031 means the paperwork side of the kitchen goes in two years and the cooking goes in five, and I'd be 32. Daniel's bus would probably go around the same time, and that's both of our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop spending on anything big, so no holiday next summer, and push the savings as hard as I could. In the first year after AGI, I'd look at work that still needs hands and a kind face, probably care work, because my auntie does it. I'd want to see others try it before I jumped, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's going and I can watch it going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we need a plan that isn't both of us in jobs a machine can do. He'd say we'll be fine, he always does. My partner Daniel says a robot will never drive the night bus. I think he's wrong, and that scares me more than the grill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to see others try care work first. With only a few years, is there time for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the part I don't like about myself. I'm someone who waits until a thing is proven. In this picture, waiting might mean I'm the last one through the door.

say: I'd say it's **scary** and leave it there, because I avoid arguments online.
At work we'd all repeat that someone **still has to cook**.
think: Privately I'd be counting: **two years** for the paperwork side, **five** for the cooking itself.
My partner's **bus job** could go at the same time, taking **both wages** at once.
do: Cancel next summer's **holiday** and stop all big spending straight away.
Push **savings** as hard as possible before the robots reach kitchens in 2031.
Look into **care work** through her aunt in the first year after AGI.
feel: She feels **sick**, as if the floor is going and she can watch it.
S2.quote: My partner Daniel says a robot will never drive the night bus. I think he's wrong, and that scares me more than the grill.
fieldNote: The **two-earner risk** drives her fear more than her own grill station does.
She sees her own **wait-until-proven** habit as a weakness when time is this short.
She counts the **three-year gap** before robots as real but too short to retrain slowly.

steps.text: Cancel next summer's holiday and skip any big purchases
Put every spare bit of pay into savings before 2031
Ask the aunt who does care work how to get a job there

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them. That's the sensible thing to say and I'd mean it. You'd hear more people at work talking about courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side and eight for the robots is long enough that I'd actually do something. I'd be 35 when the robots come to kitchens. The worry is that the owner buys one early, the moment it's cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years, I'd do an evening course in food safety and kitchen management, because someone still has to sign off and be responsible. Once AGI arrived in 2031, I'd see what the other cooks were doing and follow the ones it was working for. Daniel and I would also stop talking about a bigger flat and save instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's the kind of worry you can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why management rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched Marco's job. Half of it is people: sorting out fights, covering sick days, calming the owner down. A robot might sear a steak, but I can't see one calming down a crying junior cook on a Saturday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the bigger flat, how much does giving that up hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. We'd planned to move next year so we each had a room for our things. It can wait, a flat can always wait.

say: I'd say there are **a few years**, so people should use them.
I'd expect to hear more talk of **courses** around the kitchen.
think: Privately, **eight years** before kitchen robots feels long enough to actually act.
The fear is the owner buying a robot **early**, the moment it costs less than her.
do: Take an evening course in **kitchen management** and food safety within two years.
Watch which cooks find work after 2031 and **follow what works**.
Drop the **bigger flat** plan and save the difference.
feel: **Worried**, but in a way she feels she can act on.
S3.quote: A robot might sear a steak, but I can't see one calming down a crying junior cook on a Saturday night.
fieldNote: She picks **management** because she has watched how much of her head chef's job is people.
Five years turns her from frozen to **planning**, though she still wants others to go first.
Giving up the **bigger flat** is her first real household sacrifice in the interview.

steps.text: Take an evening course in kitchen management and food safety
Watch which cooks find work after 2031 and copy them
Drop the bigger flat and save the rent difference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time and people should calm down. Then I'd probably add that ten years goes quickly. Everyone in a kitchen knows how fast a year goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be 37 when AGI arrives and 40 when the robots get to kitchens around 2039, which is a strange age to start over. But ten years is enough to work my way up to head chef somewhere and get out of the hottest part of the job. Being hands-on gives me those extra three years, and I'd use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now, I'd keep cooking and aim for sous chef, then head chef within five years. Around 2036, when AGI arrives, I'd move towards the management side or teaching at the catering college, because by then I'd have the experience. Savings would stay steady, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. There's time, but there's an end date too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned teaching at the college. Have you thought about that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old tutor at the catering college said years ago that I'd be good at it. I laughed at him. In this picture, I'd probably email him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change any plans with Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe children, honestly, we've talked about trying around 30. I wouldn't want to have a baby the same year a robot takes my job and another one takes my partner's.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty and people should calm down.
Then I'd admit that in a kitchen, **a year goes fast**.
think: Privately, being **40** when kitchen robots arrive feels like an awkward age to restart.
Ten years is enough to climb to **head chef** and out of the hottest work.
do: Aim for **sous chef** soon and head chef within five years.
Email her old tutor about **teaching** at the catering college around 2036.
Keep **savings** steady without any dramatic cuts.
feel: **Uneasy**, because there is time but also a clear end date.
S4.quote: I wouldn't want to have a baby the same year a robot takes my job and another one takes my partner's.
fieldNote: With a decade, she treats **promotion** as her protection rather than leaving cooking.
The **teaching** idea comes from an old tutor's compliment she once laughed off.
Her decision about **children** is the one plan she ties directly to automation timing.

steps.text: Keep cooking and aim for head chef within five years
Email the old catering tutor about teaching at the college
Hold off on a baby until both jobs look clearer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. It's not just the robots, it's that Daniel and I would both be in the firing line in the same few years, and I'm slow to jump. What would help is someone paying for retraining while you're still working, like evening courses with your wages covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the owner. Everyone talks about what the robots can do, but the one who decides if I keep my job is the man who owns the steakhouse.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about what the robots can do, but the one who decides if I keep my job is the man who owns the steakhouse.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old grill cook** at a busy steakhouse near a train station, finishing around midnight.
She lives with her partner Daniel, a **bus driver**, and they have about **three months** of bills saved.
She calls herself good but **not the best**, and waits until change is proven before acting.
Plateau and Steady Disruption barely touch her, but **AGI by 2028** frightens her because both household jobs could go together.
With ten years, she would climb to head chef and move towards **management or teaching**.
biggestWorry: In **AGI by 2028**, she and her partner could both lose hands-on jobs within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while still working, such as evening courses with **wages covered**.
